explanations.explanation: Verse 30 says there was loud wailing in Egypt, "for there was no house without someone dead." I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story, and it's okay to let it be heavy for a moment. The sound that night was grief, spreading through the whole land.

Thunder shows up in Egypt earlier, when the LORD sent thunder and hail (Exodus 9:23). That's not the sound in this verse, though. Here the text says there was loud wailing in Egypt. I think the night was heavy, and the verse gives us a sound of grief, not a storm.

The text doesn't mention any fighting that night. What it says is that there was loud wailing in Egypt, because there was no house without someone dead. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story. The sound the verse gives us is grief.

explanations.answer: Get up and leave my people
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh, Egypt's king, tells Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), "Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested." Back in Exodus 5:2 he said he would not let Israel go. I think he was done bargaining, friend. Now he's the one doing the pushing.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, doesn't ask Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), to wait for anything. He says, "Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites!" Nobody says "Get up!" and then "Take your time." It's still night, and he wants them gone.

explanations.answer: Worship your God here in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh, Egypt's king, did once say something like that, back when he told them to sacrifice to their God in the land (Exodus 8:25). Not this time. Now he tells Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), "Go, worship the LORD as you have requested." The offer to stay is gone.

Verse 32 has Pharaoh saying, "Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart!" That's a big change. Earlier he told them that their flocks and herds had to stay behind (Exodus 10:24). Now the animals are going too.

It's actually True, friend. Pharaoh says, "Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart!" (Exodus 12:32) Earlier he wanted the flocks and herds left behind (Exodus 10:24). Same Pharaoh, new answer.

He ends with, "And bless me also." (Exodus 12:32) Think about that. Back in Exodus 5:2 Pharaoh said, "I do not know the LORD," and now he's asking Moses and Aaron for a blessing as he sends them off. That's quite a turn.
Pharaoh did once try to keep Israel's children behind and let only the men go (Exodus 10:11). Not here. In this verse he says, "And bless me also." The only thing he asks for is a blessing.

The three-day journey shows up earlier, when Moses and Aaron asked Pharaoh to let them take one into the wilderness (Exodus 5:3). Pharaoh doesn't ask them to come back at all. His last words to them are, "And bless me also." (Exodus 12:32)

The Egyptians urge the people on and say, "For otherwise… we are all going to die!" (Exodus 12:33) After a night like that, I think they were scared. They weren't waiting around for a second invitation. Imagine somebody holding the door open and pointing.

The text doesn't say anything about starving. The Egyptians say, "For otherwise… we are all going to die!" (Exodus 12:33) That's the whole fear in one word. They want Israel out and they want them out quickly.

There's no water in this verse at all, friend. The Egyptians say, "For otherwise… we are all going to die!" (Exodus 12:33) That's what has them hurrying the people out. Hold onto that thought, because this road isn't done yet.

explanations.answer: In kneading bowls on their shoulders
explanations.explanation: Verse 34 says the people took their dough before it was leavened, carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing. My mustache handles cookie boxes all day, but a whole bowl of dough? I'd have dough all over my chef's hat. These folks were on the move.

explanations.answer: In clay jars on their donkeys
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention jars or donkeys here. It says the people took their dough "…carrying it on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing." (Exodus 12:34) So it's the bowls they carried themselves. That's a lot of dough riding on a person's shoulders.

explanations.answer: In baskets loaded on their carts
explanations.explanation: No baskets and no carts in this verse. The people carried the dough "…on their shoulders in kneading bowls wrapped in clothing." (Exodus 12:34) They wrapped the bowls up and put them on their shoulders. It's a picture of people leaving in a hurry.

It's actually False. The Israelites asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. Then "…the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request." (Exodus 12:35-36) The Egyptians said yes, not no.

The Israelites asked for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing, and the Egyptians said yes (Exodus 12:35-36). The text says, "In this way they plundered the Egyptians." That's the opposite of being turned down, baker.

explanations.answer: The LORD gave the people favor with them
explanations.explanation: Verse 36 says, "…the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request." The Egyptians weren't pushed into it by a clever sales pitch. The LORD gave the favor, and that's the whole reason.

explanations.answer: Pharaoh ordered them to hand it over
explanations.explanation: The text never says Pharaoh gave that order. What it does say is that "…the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request." (Exodus 12:36) The Israelites asked, and the Egyptians agreed. It all came from the favor the LORD gave.

explanations.answer: Moses promised to pay them back later
explanations.explanation: No promise like that appears anywhere in the passage. The Israelites acted on Moses' word and asked, and then the text says "…the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request." (Exodus 12:35-36) The reason given is the favor from the LORD. No payback plan needed.

Verse 37 says the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth. The text adds that there were about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children. That's a LOT of people on the move, and I bet somebody in that crowd was already wondering if they were there yet.

Bethel is where Jacob, Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), had a dream and named the place (Genesis 28:12, 19). It isn't where they're going here. The text says the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth.

Hebron is where Abram, whom God later renamed Abraham (Genesis 17:5), lived by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 13:18). But that isn't the place named here. Verse 37 says the Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth.

The text says about 600,000 men on foot, "…besides women and children." (Exodus 12:37) Count the women and children too, and it's even bigger. I'd need a LOT of cookie boxes just to say hello to this crowd.
It's bigger than that, friend. Verse 37 says about 600,000 men on foot, "…besides women and children." Sixty thousand is only a tenth of it. Add the women and children and the number keeps growing.
That's far short. The text says about 600,000 men on foot, "…besides women and children." (Exodus 12:37) Six thousand wouldn't even fill the front of this line. This is a whole people on the move.
It's actually False. Verse 38 says, "…a mixed multitude also went up with them…" So the crowd wasn't only Israelites. Others joined the road, along with the flocks and herds.

Verse 38 says, "…a mixed multitude also went up with them, along with great droves of livestock, both flocks and herds." So not everyone on that road was an Israelite. The text doesn't say more about who they were. It just says they went up too.

It's actually False. Verse 39 says the people "…had not prepared any provisions for themselves." They were driven out so fast that they couldn't delay, so they baked the dough they carried out into unleavened loaves. Picture a big cookie order being due right now while the flour is still in the bag. That's how fast they had to move.

The text says the people "…had not prepared any provisions for themselves." (Exodus 12:39) Their dough had no leaven, so they baked what they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened loaves. I've scrambled to finish a batch before the timer, but never with a deadline like this.

explanations.answer: They were driven out and couldn’t delay
explanations.explanation: Verse 39 says, "For when they had been driven out of Egypt, they could not delay…" Think about the morning you're running late and you leave with one shoe and half a plan. Now make that a whole nation. I've baked under pressure, but nobody handed me a deadline like that. The rush is why the provisions never got prepared.

explanations.answer: They thought Egypt would send supplies
explanations.explanation: The text never says they expected anything like that. Verse 39 says, "For when they had been driven out of Egypt, they could not delay and had not prepared any provisions for themselves." The reason was the rush. They couldn't delay.

explanations.answer: Moses told them to travel light
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Moses told them that. Verse 39 says, "…they could not delay and had not prepared any provisions for themselves." They were driven out, and there was no time. Traveling light wasn't a plan this time.
Verse 41 says, "At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt." To the very day, friend. After 430 years, the text still counts the day.

It's actually True. Verse 41 says, "At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt." That's 430 years, and then the very day. I've missed a timer by two minutes, so this is humbling.

explanations.answer: All the Israelites for generations to come
explanations.explanation: Verse 42 says this same night "…is to be a vigil to the LORD, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come." It's not a night for a few. It's for everyone, and it keeps going down the generations.

explanations.answer: Only the priests and Levites each year
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't limit it to any group like that. It says the night is "…to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come." (Exodus 12:42) All of them. Not a few.

explanations.answer: Only Moses and Aaron that first year
explanations.explanation: That's too small. Verse 42 says the night is "…to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come." So it's all the Israelites, and it goes on far past that first year.

Verse 50 says, "Then all the Israelites did this—they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron." Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother (Exodus 4:14), were the ones who received the command. The people did just what He said.
It's actually True, friend. Verse 50 says, "…they did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron." The people did what they were told. Everything the LORD commanded, they did.
